choices.E:
\(1\) cannot be represented as a sum of finitely many special
numbers

routes.label: Divide by 7 and count decimal digits

question: Call a positive real number special if it has a decimal representation that consists entirely of digits \(0\) and \(7.\) For example, \(\frac{700}{99}=7.\overline{07}=7.070707\ldots\) and \(77.007\) are special numbers. What is the smallest \(n\) such that \(1\) can be written as a sum of \(n\) special numbers?
solution:
Dividing by \(7\) turns the allowed digits \(0\) and \(7\) into \(0\) and \(1\), making decimal addition easier to control. Every special summand of \(1\) must have integer part \(0\): a nonzero integer part using only the allowed digits would make that summand at least \(7\).

Suppose \(n\leq 7\) special numbers sum to \(1\). After dividing each summand by \(7\), we obtain \(n\) decimals using only digits \(0\) and \(1\), whose sum is \(1/7\). Each decimal column contains at most seven ones, so no carrying occurs. Their sum therefore has a decimal representation using only digits \(0\) through \(7\). However, long division gives
\[
\frac17=0.\overline{142857},
\]
which contains an \(8\). This number has no terminating decimal representation, so its decimal expansion is unique. Thus \(n\geq 8\).

To construct eight summands, let \(d_k\) be the digit in the \(k\)th decimal place of \(1/7\). Construct eight numbers \(y_1,\ldots,y_8\) as follows: put a \(1\) in the \(k\)th decimal place of \(y_i\) when \(i\leq d_k\), and put a \(0\) there otherwise. For example, the first column has a \(1\) only in \(y_1\), the second has ones in \(y_1,\ldots,y_4\), and the fourth has ones in all eight numbers.

Each column then sums to exactly \(d_k\), with no carrying, so
\[
y_1+\cdots+y_8=\frac17.
\]
All eight numbers are positive because their fourth decimal digits are \(1\). Multiplying each by \(7\) replaces every \(1\) by \(7\), producing eight special numbers whose sum is \(1\). Therefore the smallest possible number is \(\boxed{8}\), choice \(\mathrm{B}\).
